span.term: learn distributed word vectors with a shallow model - CBOW predicts a word from its context, skip-gram predicts the context from the word - so words in similar contexts get similar vectors
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: for many languages the available training corpora are only a few billion words or less (a data constraint)
span.note: what this limits: the results for lower-resource languages: Quotation withheld
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The exact-match accuracy metric makes 100% unreachable because the models have no morphological information and synonyms count as errors.
span.note: what this limits: the accuracy figures against their own ceiling: REACHING 100% ACCURACY IS LIKELY TO BE IMPOSSIBLE, AS THE CURRENT MODELS DO NOT HAVE ANY INPUT INFORMATION ABOUT WORD MORPHOLOGY
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The test set excludes multi-word entities.
span.note: what this limits: everything the evaluation can speak about: WE HAVE INCLUDED IN OUR TEST SET ONLY SINGLE TOKEN WORDS, THUS MULTI-WORD ENTITIES ARE NOT PRESENT (SUCH AS NEW YORK) - what falls outside is invisible, not wrong
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Relationship accuracy in the qualitative examples still leaves much room for improvement.
span.note: what this limits: the qualitative relationship examples: ACCURACY IS QUITE GOOD, ALTHOUGH THERE IS CLEARLY A LOT OF ROOM FOR FURTHER IMPROVEMENTS
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: On the Microsoft Sentence Completion Challenge the Skip-gram model alone is worse than LSA similarity; it only wins in combination with RNNLMs.
span.note: what this limits: the Sentence Completion result specifically: THE SKIP-GRAM MODEL ITSELF DOES NOT PERFORM ON THIS TASK BETTER THAN LSA SIMILARITY - it contributes only in combination
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The benchmark's question count is combinatorial: questions are formed by pairing items from short hand-made lists, so the number of questions is far larger than the number of independent facts being tested.
span.note: what this limits: the size of this test set as a measure of evidence: a list of 68 hand-listed American cities and their states was expanded into about 2,500 questions by pairing entries at random, so questions within a category are not independent of one another
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: In the semantic half of a semantic benchmark, a correct-meaning answer is scored wrong unless it is the exact expected token.
span.note: what this limits: any accuracy figure from this test set: the answer must be the exact expected token, and synonyms are counted as mistakes
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The connection between the benchmark and any practical use is asserted as a belief, not shown.
span.note: what this limits: this accuracy as evidence that the vectors are useful: the authors state a belief that usefulness for certain applications should be positively correlated with the metric
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.
